In a typical electrolyte, the solubility of solute usually decreases dramatically as the temperature drops, so as the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte. This is governed by $\Delta G_{sol}$ , which is build up by $\Delta H_{sol}$ and $\Delta S_{sol}$ through the combination of the 1st and 2nd laws of thermodynamic. $^{[13,14]}$ To achieve a decent low-temperature electrolyte, a favourable $\Delta G_{sol}$ over a wide temperature range is required to maintain high solubility of the salt, which is clearly determined by the competition between $\Delta H_{sol}$ (a more positive value leads to a lower solubility) and $\Delta S_{sol}$ (a larger value increases the solubility). In conventional electrolyte, the solvation of ions proceeds favourably at room temperature regardless of solvent's strong or weak solvation capability toward salt. Under low temperature, however, severe aggregation of ions or solvent molecules and consequently its increased degree of order (or $\Delta S < 0$ ) leads to the formation of heterogeneous system, i.e., the precipitation of salt, which drastically deteriorates the electrolyte property, as shown in Figure 1a. Our design principle of low-temperature electrolyte is, therefore, put forward to avoid salt precipitation while still maintaining high stability of the electrolyte against the electrodes during (dis)charge. We argue that tuning the solvation structure through introducing solvents with various solvation capability could enhance the solubility of salt by decreasing the system degree of order ( $\Delta S > 0$ ) at low temperature. More specifically, mixing an SS solvent and a WS solvent could have more diverse solvation structure that is capable of altering spontaneously in response to the temperature dropping, and thus, realizing a temperature-adaptive electrolyte (Figure 1b).

- Salt concentration 0.8 mol/L NaPF6：The source's ECC formulation is explicitly given as 0.8 M NaPF6 in EC/PC/EMC, matching the candidate's 0.8 M NaPF6 concentration. [0002_Cai 等 - 2024 - A dual-functional electrolyte additive for stabilizing the solid electrolyte interphase and solvatio::sec7::child9]
- Solvent composition EC/PC/EMC with PC as the dominant component (ratios ~1:4:1)：The source describes ECC electrolyte with EC/PC/EMC = 0.5:2:0.5 (i.e., 1:4:1), which is equivalent to the candidate's EC:PC:EMC = 0.1667:0.6667:0.1667; EC is partially replaced by PC to obtain better cycle performance, consistent with the candidate's PC-rich ratio. - NaDFP additive present：The source repeatedly evaluates a NaDFP dual-functional additive, showing cells with NaDFP exhibit improved capacity retention and less anodic decomposition, supporting NaDFP as the additive identified in the candidate. - Evidence for low-temperature (-20 C) operation of the candidate electrolyte：The sources only report measurements at elevated temperatures (60 C shelving/cycling, 45 C ICP-OES); no low-temperature or -20 C data are provided, so the candidate's low-temperature suitability is not established from the literature. - Reversible no-plating capacity limit determined for the target full cell：No source reports a no-plating (sodium plating threshold) capacity limit, nor any plating/reversibility measurement, so this target metric is unaddressed. 
- Full cell configuration Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3||hard-carbon：The sources address NFM cathodes with hard-carbon anodes; the Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 cathode of the target cell is not studied, so evidence does not cover the target full cell identity. source_refs.raw_quote: Coin cells (CR2032) were used to test the electrochemical performances. 1M NaClO $_{4}$ solution in a mixture of ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume) was applied as the electrolyte for the half cell and full cells. Two pieces of Whatman glass fibers soaked with the electrolyte were used as the separator between the positive and negative electrode. The HC electrode was prepared by casting a slurry of 90 wt% HC, 5 wt% conductive carbon black and 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder on copper foil. In companions, electrodes using carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) and sodium alginate (NaAg) as the binder were also prepared. Typical loading mass of the HC electrode was around 1.5 mg cm $^{-2}$ . For the full cell, Na $_{3.5}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{2}$ F $_{3}$ powders were mixed with 20% carbon SP for the preparation of positive electrodes. The weight ratio of the positive/negative electrodes was 2.5. The cells were galvanostatic charged/discharged with a LAND 2001 CT battery test system (Wuhan, China) under various voltage ranges and current rates. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a VMP system (Biologic S.A., Claix, France).

source_refs.raw_quote: In view of this, there are few studies for low temperature NIBs using hard carbon as the anode. Instead, more attention is attracted to the alloy or carbon/alloy composite for their adequate capacity of around 100 mAh g $^{-1}$ at low temperatures, such as Ti-based metal oxides, $^{[16,17]}$ , Se/graphene $^{[18]}$ and Sb/CNT $^{[19]}$ composites. However, these anode materials are accompanied by the high average voltage, which is detrimental to the energy density of the full cell. Previous work indicates that the capacity of hard carbon may be fully utilized by lowering the cut-off potential to below 0 V. $^{[20]}$ It indeed allows a high capacity of 265 mAh g $^{-1}$ at -15 °C, $^{[21]}$ although the possibility of Na plating requires prudent investigation. In this work, the calcination protocol of synthesizing HC from biomass waste is systematically explored. It shows a significant dependence of the performance on the heat treatment processes. The optimized HC was then evaluated at both the room and low-temperature. Assisted with the in situ and ex situ XRD, the possibility of Na metal plating is thoroughly examined. A safe and reversible capacity of 250 mAh g $^{-1}$ at -20 °C for HC is obtained without Na plating in HC. Furthermore, a $Na_{3.5}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{2}F_{3}$ cathode was prepared to couple with HC for investigating the low temperature behaviors of HC in full cell, which has been rarely studied.

source_refs.raw_quote: One may still argue the accuracy of in situ XRD tests as the signal of metallic Na would not be detectable until the amount is accumulated to a specific value. In order to determine the Na plating capacity more punctually, ex situ XRD is conducted on HC electrodes in coin cells with capacity limitation from 200 to $300\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ . The cells were cycled for 10 cycles to accumulate potential metallic Na. XRD patterns were collected at a discharged state. As shown in Figure S4, no Na peak is observed beneath the capacity of $250\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ , and the Na signal appeared in $300\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ sample. The Coulombic efficiency provides implications. The average Coulombic efficiency is around $97.4\%$ for the cells cycling at a limited capacity of $250\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ or less. The value is close to $97.8\%$ when the cell is tested at room temperature with a cut-off voltage of 0 V. For the cell cycled at $300\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ , the Coulombic efficiency decreases to only $95.3\%$ due to the Na plating/stripping.

source_refs.raw_quote: The voltage profiles of $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}/\mathrm{HC}$ full cell consists of a plateau at 4.1 V and sloping regime between 3.6-2.5 V, contributing to an accumulative capacity of 306 mAh g $^{-1}$ (based on the mass of anode). The energy density is calculated to be 310 Wh kg $^{-1}$ based on the total weight of cathode and anode, along with an average discharge potential of 3.62 V. A stable cyclic performance similar to that in half-cell is achieved at $25^{\circ}$ C, as indicated by full cell F1 in Figure 5b. Ulteriorly, we tested the behavior of full cell under low temperature. Firstly, the performance of $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}$ half-cell at 0°C and -20°C are measured and given in Figure S7a and S7b. The reversible capacity decreases with lowering the temperature. It maintains 93.2% and 80.4% of the capacity at room temperature for testing at 0°C and -20°C, respectively. Nevertheless, cyclic stability is kept. It is worthwhile to mention that the safe capacity for HC working at -20°C is 250 mAh g $^{-1}$ , which is also around 80% of its capacity at room temperature. Therefore, there is no need to change the mass ratio of the cathode and anode in the full cell for operating at low temperature.

As expected, the $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}/\mathrm{HC}$ full cell also demonstrates a capacity reduction at 0 °C in the first several cycles and reaches stable capacity retention of 244 mAh g $^{-1}$ (F2 in Figure 5b). However, when the full cell was charged/discharged at -20°C, a significant drop in capacity is observed, particularly during the first 5 cycles. It may lie in the increased resistance on the anode side as reflected by EIS. The dynamic property of $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}/\mathrm{HC}$ at different temperatures is also evaluated using galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT), as indicated in Figure 5c. From the calculation, the diffusion coefficient of Na-ions ( $D_{Na}^{+}$ ) at 25°C is in the range of $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-10}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ . The value is only slightly decreased at 0°C. In sharp contrast, the $D_{Na}^{+}$ value is about one magnitude lower at -25 °C than that at 25°C. The slow $Na^{+}$ diffusion is in agreement with the EIS results that the thicker SEI film would affect the ion diffusion. After testing at $-20^{\circ}C$ for 10 cycles, the same cell (F3) was put back to $25^{\circ}C$ and its capacity gradually recovered and regained ca. 82% of the capacity at $25^{\circ}C$ .

source_refs.raw_quote: This work aims to demonstrate the critical effect of electrode-electrolyte interfacial chemistry on the performance of a commercial hard carbon anode operating at the rate and temperature extremes. A new weakly solvating electrolyte (WSE) consisting of a cyclic ether (tetrahydrofuran, THF) as solvent and $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ as the electrolyte salt was proposed to optimize the interfacial properties of anode/electrolyte. Surprisingly, the lower ion desolvation energy and homogeneous SEI are simultaneously achieved. Benefiting from the low $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ desolvation energy and fast transport at the anode/electrolyte interface, the commercial hard carbon anode demonstrates ultra-high rate capability and remarkable low-temperature performance.

source_refs.raw_quote: It is well known that low-temperature performance is also significant for some special scenarios in practical applications. However, there are few reports on the low-temperature performance of the HC anode for SIBs. As previous studies have indicated that the solvation structure of the electrolyte defines the charge-transfer behavior at low temperature, $^{[13a]}$ the low-temperature performance of HC in THF-based electrolyte was further investigated. When the ambient temperature drops to $-5^{\circ}C$ (Figure 5a), the specific capacities of HC in 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ /THF electrolyte at 20 mA g $^{-1}$ and 5 Ag $^{-1}$ are 282 and 155 mAh g $^{-1}$ , respectively, indicating superior rate capability. Even at -20°C, a high capacity of 269 and 175 mAh g $^{-1}$ can be achieved at 20 mA g $^{-1}$ and 2 Ag $^{-1}$ , respectively. The charge-discharge profile in 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ /THF electrolyte (Figure 5b,c) still maintains a high low-plateau capacity at different densities, indicating favorable kinetics. Moreover, HC anode in 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ /THF electrolyte also possesses superior long-term cycling stability with a specific capacity of 203 mAh g $^{-1}$ over 1000 cycles at a large current density of 2 A g $^{-1}$ at -5°C (Figure 5d). Even at a lower temperature of -20°C, it still delivers high capacity retention up to 95% with a specific capacity of 181 mAh g $^{-1}$ over 1000 cycles (Figure 5e).

source_refs.raw_quote: To reveal the influence of the ion–solvent structure on the performance of the anode, commercial hard carbon (HC), which is the most promising anode material, was employed as an example. The morphology and structure details of commercial hard carbon are demonstrated in Figures S2 and S3. Figure 2a shows the rate capability of HC in different electrolytes. As seen, it delivers capacities of 304 and $300\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ at a current density of $20\ mA\ g^{-1}$ in $NaPF_{6}/PC$ and $NaPF_{6}/EC/DEC$ electrolytes, respectively. However, they sharply decrease to $<100\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ when the current density is above $200\ mA\ g^{-1}$ . Interestingly, the rate capability of HC in $NaPF_{6}/THF$ and $NaPF_{6}/DME$ electrolytes is much superior. As seen, the HC electrode demonstrates the best rate capability in the $NaPF_{6}/THF$ electrolyte with 305, 277, 266, 260, 250 and $238\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ at current densities of 20, 100, 200, 500, 1000 and $2000\ mA\ g^{-1}$ , respectively. Even at $5000\ mA\ g^{-1}$ ( $20\ C,\ 1\ C=250\ mA\ g^{-1}$ ), a high discharge capacity of $212\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ is still maintained for the THF solvent, which is much higher than those of DME (193 mAh g $^{-1}$ ), PC (24 mAh g $^{-1}$ ) and EC/DEC (5 mAh g $^{-1}$ ) solvents.

source_refs.raw_quote: Figure 1a and Table S1 (Supporting Information) present the temperature-dependent ionic conductivities of the dilute NaPF $_{6}$ -based ether electrolyte (0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ in DEGDME, 0.5-P-D), the conventional concentration NaPF $_{6}$ -based ether electrolyte (1.0 M NaPF $_{6}$ in DEGDME, 1.0-P-D), and the commercial ester-based electrolyte (1.0 M NaPF $_{6}$ in the mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC) and dimethyl carbonate (DMC) with a volume ratio of 1:1, 1.0-P-E/M). At 25 °C, 0.5-P-D exhibits a lower ionic conductivity (2.7 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) compared to 1.0-P-D (7.3 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) and 1.0-P-E/M (15.3 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) due to its low salt concentration. Over the temperature range from 25 to -50 °C, all three electrolytes display a negative correlation between ionic conductivity and temperature. source_refs.raw_quote: We argue that tuning the solvation structure through introducing solvents with various solvation capability could enhance the solubility of salt by decreasing the system degree of order ( $\Delta S > 0$ ) at low temperature. More specifically, mixing an SS solvent and a WS solvent could have more diverse solvation structure that is capable of altering spontaneously in response to the temperature dropping, and thus, realizing a temperature-adaptive electrolyte (Figure 1b). As a proof of concept, we selected $NaPF_{6}$ as a representative salt to pair with an SS–WS ether solvent mixture. To minimize any potential impact of $\varepsilon$ and DN on the solvation structure, DIG and tetrahydrofuran (THF) solvents with similar $\varepsilon$ (7.23 vs 7.58) and DN (19.5 vs 20.0 kcal mol $^{-1}$ ) values, $^{[15,16]}$ were specifically chosen as the SS and WS solvents, respectively (Table S1, Supporting Information). We first optimized our proposed SS–WS electrolyte formulation to 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in DIG and THF (2:8 in volume ratio, denoted as NDT, Figure S5, Supporting Information). To compare, 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in THF (denoted as NT) was chosen as the WS electrolyte and 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in DIG (denoted as ND) as the SS electrolyte. We then used density functional theory (DFT) calculations to determine the binding energies $(E_{\mathrm{b}})$ of cation–solvent complexes based on the optimized geometrical structures (Figure S1, Supporting Information).

2.4. Toward Practical Viability
We have also examined the compatibility of NDT electrolyte against high-voltage cathode materials for Na-ion batteries. A P2-type $Na_{2/3}Ni_{1/4}Cu_{1/12}Mn_{2/3}O_{2}$ (NNCM) cathode (Figure S16, Supporting Information) was selected as cathode materials to pair with Na metal anode in NDT electrolyte to assembled coin cells. With temperature dropping to -40 and -50 °C, NNCM cathode still achieves quite decent capacities of 79.7 and 72.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ , respectively, corresponding to 88.8% and 81.0% of the capacity delivered at 25 °C (Figure S17a, Supporting Information). Equally importantly, NNCM cathode demonstrated encouraging cycling stability and rate performance in NDT electrolytes under low-temperature operation. For instance, a high-capacity retention of 99.9% over 100 cycles with average columbic efficiency of 99.8% is achieved at -40 °C (Figure S17b, Supporting Information). Even at high rate of 2C, the NNCM cathode still retains reversible capacities of 74.5 mAh g $^{-1}$ (84.2% of that at 0.1 C, see Figure S17c, Supporting Information) at -40 °C. To further verify the feasibility of NDT electrolyte in practical cells, full cells with NNCM cathode and hard carbon anode were fabricated and cycled within 1.50–3.65 V at various temperatures. The NNCM||hard carbon cell delivers an initial discharge capacity of 71.2 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 25 °C, while 70.2% of that capacity can be maintained when the temperature decreases to -40 °C (Figure S18, Supporting Information). In addition, the NNCM||hard carbon full cell exhibits much enhanced cycling stability at -40 °C by featuring a 90.6% capacity retention after 400 cycles (Figure S17d, Supporting Information). Clearly, our testing data demonstrated NDT electrolyte is fully compatible with layered oxide cathode and hard carbon anode, and thus, showed great potential for practical applications in Na-ion battery.

Miaomiao Xia, Hui Chen, Zhenxu Zheng, Qingfei Meng, $^{*}$ Along Zhao, Xiaoyang Chen, Xinping Ai, Yongjin Fang, $^{*}$ and Yuliang Cao $^{*}$

Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) are emerging as a promising alternative for next-generation energy storage solutions, driven by the economic and environmental benefits of abundant sodium resources. A pivotal aspect of SIB advancement is the development of advanced electrolytes, which remains a formidable challenge. Herein, a facile and scalable synthesis method for low-cost sodium-difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB) is reported and explored its application as a standalone electrolyte salt for SIBs. The NaDFOB-based ether electrolyte demonstrates exceptional electrochemical stability, solvent compatibility, and the unique capacity to form a dense, robust solid-electrolyte interphase layer on electrode surfaces. As a result, the $\mathrm{Na_{4}Fe_{3}(PO_{4})_{2}P_{2}O_{7}}$ (NFPP) cathode with NaDFOB-based electrolyte exhibits ultrahigh cycling stability with a remarkable capacity retention of 98.7% after 1000 cycles. Furthermore, an Ah-level hard carbon (HC)//NFPP pouch cell using NaDFOB-based ether electrolyte shows an impressive cycle life of 500 cycles, coupled with an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.9%. The pouch cells also maintain superior electrochemical performance across a broad temperature range from -40 to 60 °C, showcasing the electrolyte's versatility.

Zheng Tang $^{+}$ , Hong Wang $^{+}$ , Peng-Fei Wu, Si-Yu Zhou, Yuan-Cheng Huang, Rui Zhang, Dan Sun, $^{*}$ You-Gen Tang, and Hai-Yan Wang $^{*}$

Abstract: Sodium-ion batteries capable of operating at rate and temperature extremes are highly desirable, but elusive due to the dynamics and thermodynamics limitations. Herein, a strategy of electrode-electrolyte interfacial chemistry modulation is proposed. The commercial hard carbon demonstrates superior rate performance with $212\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ at an ultra-high current density of $5\ A\ g^{-1}$ in the electrolyte with weak ion solvation/desolvation, which is much higher than those in common electrolytes (nearly no capacity in carbonate-based electrolytes). Even at $-20^{\circ}C$ , a high capacity of $175\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ (74% of its room-temperature capacity) can be maintained at $2\ A\ g^{-1}$ . Such an electrode retains 90% of its initial capacity after 1000 cycles. As proven, weak ion solvation/desolvation of tetrahydrofuran greatly facilitates fast-ion diffusion at the SEI/electrolyte interface and homogeneous SEI with well-distributed NaF and organic components ensures fast $Na^{+}$ diffusion through the SEI layer and a stable interface.

source_refs.raw_quote: In summary, we have demonstrated that electrode-electrolyte interphase chemistry including ion desolvation and SEI interphase are crucial to the electrochemical properties of the anode at the ultra-high rate and low-temperature extremes via the comparative study of different electrolytes. The THF-based electrolyte enables the commercial HC anode superior rate capability (up to $5 \, Ag^{-1}$ ) and ultra-low-temperature performance (operating stably at $-20^{\circ}C$ ). Kinetic analysis reveals that the remarkable performance is attributed to weakly $Na^{+}$ -solvent desolvation energy and uniform SEI composition achieved in the THF-based electrolyte, which is beneficial to the ion diffusion between the electrolyte–electrode interface and interface stability. This work not only proposes an advanced low-temperature electrolyte, but also provides new insights into the interfacial modulation for next-generation high-rate and low-temperature batteries.

source_refs.raw_quote: For example, $NaClO_{4}$ is very explosive and its adsorbed $H_{2}O$ is too difficult to dry out. $^{[28]}$ $NaPF_{6}$ is toxic and expensive, easy to decompose at elevated temperatures and under humidity. $^{[5,14]}$ The NaTFSI and NaFSI are of high cost, and the $TFSI^{-}$ (or $FSI^{-}$ ) anion in NaTFSI (or NaFSI) has a corrosive effect on the aluminum foil collector. $^{[8]}$ Thus, it is of great significance to explore advanced salts to promote the wide applicability of SIBs. Sodium difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB), which has non-localized electrons in the structure and weak bonds between sodium-ions and anions, has shown fascinating properties, such as high conductivity, compatibility with a variety of solvents, and own film-forming characteristics with no need for film-forming additives. $^{[14,29,30]}$ However, the use of NaDFOB as a single salt for electrolytes and their compatibility with different SIB electrodes have rarely been reported.

source_refs.raw_quote: We have thoroughly examined its application as a single salt for the electrolytes of SIBs. The NaDFOB facilitates the formation of a dense and robust cathode-electrolyte interface (CEI) layer on the $\mathrm{Na_{3}Fe_{2}(PO_{4})P_{2}O_{7}}$ (NFPP) cathode, significantly enhances its cyclability and Coulombic efficiency (CE). Specifically, the NFPP electrode demonstrates an impressive capacity retention of 98.7% after 1000 cycles along with an average CE of 99.96%. Moreover, the hard carbon (HC)//NFPP pouch cell with NaDFOB-diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (G2) electrolyte shows an extended cycling lifespan of 500 cycles and commendable low-temperature performance. Our findings contribute to the exploration of affordable and functional sodium salts, thereby advancing the practical implementation of SIBs in various applications.

As is well known, sodium salts, a medium for ion conductivity and sodium sources for sothiation/de-sothiation process, plays an essential role in determining the electrochemical performance of SIBs. Therefore,

Ming [3] et al. evaluated the properties of sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ), sodium perchlorate (NaClO $_4$ ), sodium trifluoromethanesulfonate (NaOTF) and sodium tetrafluoroborate (NaBF $_4$ ) as main salts. Among them, NaPF $_6$ was proven to have the best comprehensive performance including high solubility, high thermal stability and optimized orbital energy level. The compatibility of sodium salts and solvents/additives is considerably important for the function of the sodium salts. Generally, the solvents with additives are mainly used as a medium to transport sodium ions, affecting the conductivity and viscosity of the electrolyte, solvating the electrolyte salts, and ensuring the transmission of sodium ions. Yi et al. [4] incorporated a HC anode protected by ester-originated SEI with ether-based electrolyte, which indeed fused the merits of ester- and ether-based electrolytes and achieved a high reversibility and rate capability. Che et al. [5] systematically studied the carbonate-based electrolytes for NFM/HC SIBs and demonstrated that as compared with ethylene carbonate (EC)-based electrolyte, Propylene carbonate (PC)-based electrolytes outperform better in terms of capacity retention and safety.

citations.quote: Coin cells (CR2032) were used to test the electrochemical performances. 1M NaClO $_{4}$ solution in a mixture of ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume) was applied as the electrolyte for the half cell and full cells. Two pieces of Whatman glass fibers soaked with the electrolyte were used as the separator between the positive and negative electrode. The HC electrode was prepared by casting a slurry of 90 wt% HC, 5 wt% conductive carbon black and 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder on copper foil. In companions, electrodes using carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) and sodium alginate (NaAg) as the binder were also prepared. Typical loading mass of the HC electrode was around 1.5 mg cm $^{-2}$ . For the full cell, Na $_{3.5}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{2}$ F $_{3}$ powders were mixed with 20% carbon SP for the preparation of positive electrodes. The weight ratio of the positive/negative electrodes was 2.5. The cells were galvanostatic charged/discharged with a LAND 2001 CT battery test system (Wuhan, China) under various voltage ranges and current rates. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a VMP system (Biologic S.A., Claix, France).

However, when the full cell was charged/discharged at -20°C, a significant drop in capacity is observed, particularly during the first 5 cycles. It may lie in the increased resistance on the anode side as reflected by EIS. The dynamic property of $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}/\mathrm{HC}$ at different temperatures is also evaluated using galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT), as indicated in Figure 5c. From the calculation, the diffusion coefficient of Na-ions ( $D_{Na}^{+}$ ) at 25°C is in the range of $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-10}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ . The value is only slightly decreased at 0°C. In sharp contrast, the $D_{Na}^{+}$ value is about one magnitude lower at -25 °C than that at 25°C. citations.quote: This work aims to demonstrate the critical effect of electrode-electrolyte interfacial chemistry on the performance of a commercial hard carbon anode operating at the rate and temperature extremes. A new weakly solvating electrolyte (WSE) consisting of a cyclic ether (tetrahydrofuran, THF) as solvent and $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ as the electrolyte salt was proposed to optimize the interfacial properties of anode/electrolyte. citations.quote: It is well known that low-temperature performance is also significant for some special scenarios in practical applications. However, there are few reports on the low-temperature performance of the HC anode for SIBs. As previous studies have indicated that the solvation structure of the electrolyte defines the charge-transfer behavior at low temperature, $^{[13a]}$ the low-temperature performance of HC in THF-based electrolyte was further investigated. When the ambient temperature drops to $-5^{\circ}C$ (Figure 5a), the specific capacities of HC in 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ /THF electrolyte at 20 mA g $^{-1}$ and 5 Ag $^{-1}$ are 282 and 155 mAh g $^{-1}$ , respectively, indicating superior rate capability. Even at -20°C, a high capacity of 269 and 175 mAh g $^{-1}$ can be achieved at 20 mA g $^{-1}$ and 2 Ag $^{-1}$ , respectively. The charge-discharge profile in 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ /THF electrolyte (Figure 5b,c) still maintains a high low-plateau capacity at different densities, indicating favorable kinetics. Moreover, HC anode in 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ /THF electrolyte also possesses superior long-term cycling stability with a specific capacity of 203 mAh g $^{-1}$ over 1000 cycles at a large current density of 2 A g $^{-1}$ at -5°C (Figure 5d). Even at a lower temperature of -20°C, it still delivers high capacity retention up to 95% with a specific capacity of 181 mAh g $^{-1}$ over 1000 cycles (Figure 5e).

Zheng Tang $^{+}$ , Hong Wang $^{+}$ , Peng-Fei Wu, Si-Yu Zhou, Yuan-Cheng Huang, Rui Zhang, Dan Sun, $^{*}$ You-Gen Tang, and Hai-Yan Wang $^{*}$

Abstract: Sodium-ion batteries capable of operating at rate and temperature extremes are highly desirable, but elusive due to the dynamics and thermodynamics limitations. Herein, a strategy of electrode-electrolyte interfacial chemistry modulation is proposed. The commercial hard carbon demonstrates superior rate performance with $212\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ at an ultra-high current density of $5\ A\ g^{-1}$ in the electrolyte with weak ion solvation/desolvation, which is much higher than those in common electrolytes (nearly no capacity in carbonate-based electrolytes). Even at $-20^{\circ}C$ , a high capacity of $175\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ (74% of its room-temperature capacity) can be maintained at $2\ A\ g^{-1}$ . Such an electrode retains 90% of its initial capacity after 1000 cycles. As proven, weak ion solvation/desolvation of tetrahydrofuran greatly facilitates fast-ion diffusion at the SEI/electrolyte interface and homogeneous SEI with well-distributed NaF and organic components ensures fast $Na^{+}$ diffusion through the SEI layer and a stable interface.

citations.quote: In summary, we have demonstrated that electrode-electrolyte interphase chemistry including ion desolvation and SEI interphase are crucial to the electrochemical properties of the anode at the ultra-high rate and low-temperature extremes via the comparative study of different electrolytes. The THF-based electrolyte enables the commercial HC anode superior rate capability (up to $5 \, Ag^{-1}$ ) and ultra-low-temperature performance (operating stably at $-20^{\circ}C$ ). Kinetic analysis reveals that the remarkable performance is attributed to weakly $Na^{+}$ -solvent desolvation energy and uniform SEI composition achieved in the THF-based electrolyte, which is beneficial to the ion diffusion between the electrolyte–electrode interface and interface stability. This work not only proposes an advanced low-temperature electrolyte, but also provides new insights into the interfacial modulation for next-generation high-rate and low-temperature batteries.

According to the above discussions, as illustrated in Figure 4c,d, the electrode–electrolyte interfacial chemistry can be well-modulated in the THF-based electrolyte. As a consequence, the commercial HC electrode can demonstrate significantly improved electrochemical properties in THF-based electrolyte in comparison to that in ester-based electrolytes.

citations.chunk_id: 0073_Yang 等 - 2023 - Entropy-Driven Solvation toward Low-Temperature Sodium-Ion Batteries with Temperature-Adaptive Featu::sec2::child1
citations.quote: We argue that tuning the solvation structure through introducing solvents with various solvation capability could enhance the solubility of salt by decreasing the system degree of order ( $\Delta S > 0$ ) at low temperature. More specifically, mixing an SS solvent and a WS solvent could have more diverse solvation structure that is capable of altering spontaneously in response to the temperature dropping, and thus, realizing a temperature-adaptive electrolyte (Figure 1b). As a proof of concept, we selected $NaPF_{6}$ as a representative salt to pair with an SS–WS ether solvent mixture. To minimize any potential impact of $\varepsilon$ and DN on the solvation structure, DIG and tetrahydrofuran (THF) solvents with similar $\varepsilon$ (7.23 vs 7.58) and DN (19.5 vs 20.0 kcal mol $^{-1}$ ) values, $^{[15,16]}$ were specifically chosen as the SS and WS solvents, respectively (Table S1, Supporting Information). We first optimized our proposed SS–WS electrolyte formulation to 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in DIG and THF (2:8 in volume ratio, denoted as NDT, Figure S5, Supporting Information). To compare, 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in THF (denoted as NT) was chosen as the WS electrolyte and 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in DIG (denoted as ND) as the SS electrolyte. We then used density functional theory (DFT) calculations to determine the binding energies $(E_{\mathrm{b}})$ of cation–solvent complexes based on the optimized geometrical structures (Figure S1, Supporting Information).

citations.quote:
2.4. Toward Practical Viability
We have also examined the compatibility of NDT electrolyte against high-voltage cathode materials for Na-ion batteries. A P2-type $Na_{2/3}Ni_{1/4}Cu_{1/12}Mn_{2/3}O_{2}$ (NNCM) cathode (Figure S16, Supporting Information) was selected as cathode materials to pair with Na metal anode in NDT electrolyte to assembled coin cells. With temperature dropping to -40 and -50 °C, NNCM cathode still achieves quite decent capacities of 79.7 and 72.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ , respectively, corresponding to 88.8% and 81.0% of the capacity delivered at 25 °C (Figure S17a, Supporting Information). Equally importantly, NNCM cathode demonstrated encouraging cycling stability and rate performance in NDT electrolytes under low-temperature operation. For instance, a high-capacity retention of 99.9% over 100 cycles with average columbic efficiency of 99.8% is achieved at -40 °C (Figure S17b, Supporting Information). Even at high rate of 2C, the NNCM cathode still retains reversible capacities of 74.5 mAh g $^{-1}$ (84.2% of that at 0.1 C, see Figure S17c, Supporting Information) at -40 °C. To further verify the feasibility of NDT electrolyte in practical cells, full cells with NNCM cathode and hard carbon anode were fabricated and cycled within 1.50–3.65 V at various temperatures. The NNCM||hard carbon cell delivers an initial discharge capacity of 71.2 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 25 °C, while 70.2% of that capacity can be maintained when the temperature decreases to -40 °C (Figure S18, Supporting Information). In addition, the NNCM||hard carbon full cell exhibits much enhanced cycling stability at -40 °C by featuring a 90.6% capacity retention after 400 cycles (Figure S17d, Supporting Information). association_citations.quote: We argue that tuning the solvation structure through introducing solvents with various solvation capability could enhance the solubility of salt by decreasing the system degree of order ( $\Delta S > 0$ ) at low temperature. More specifically, mixing an SS solvent and a WS solvent could have more diverse solvation structure that is capable of altering spontaneously in response to the temperature dropping, and thus, realizing a temperature-adaptive electrolyte (Figure 1b). As a proof of concept, we selected $NaPF_{6}$ as a representative salt to pair with an SS–WS ether solvent mixture. To minimize any potential impact of $\varepsilon$ and DN on the solvation structure, DIG and tetrahydrofuran (THF) solvents with similar $\varepsilon$ (7.23 vs 7.58) and DN (19.5 vs 20.0 kcal mol $^{-1}$ ) values, $^{[15,16]}$ were specifically chosen as the SS and WS solvents, respectively (Table S1, Supporting Information). We first optimized our proposed SS–WS electrolyte formulation to 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in DIG and THF (2:8 in volume ratio, denoted as NDT, Figure S5, Supporting Information). To compare, 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in THF (denoted as NT) was chosen as the WS electrolyte and 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in DIG (denoted as ND) as the SS electrolyte. We then used density functional theory (DFT) calculations to determine the binding energies $(E_{\mathrm{b}})$ of cation–solvent complexes based on the optimized geometrical structures (Figure S1, Supporting Information).

2.4. Toward Practical Viability
We have also examined the compatibility of NDT electrolyte against high-voltage cathode materials for Na-ion batteries. A P2-type $Na_{2/3}Ni_{1/4}Cu_{1/12}Mn_{2/3}O_{2}$ (NNCM) cathode (Figure S16, Supporting Information) was selected as cathode materials to pair with Na metal anode in NDT electrolyte to assembled coin cells. citations.quote: For example, $NaClO_{4}$ is very explosive and its adsorbed $H_{2}O$ is too difficult to dry out. $^{[28]}$ $NaPF_{6}$ is toxic and expensive, easy to decompose at elevated temperatures and under humidity. $^{[5,14]}$ The NaTFSI and NaFSI are of high cost, and the $TFSI^{-}$ (or $FSI^{-}$ ) anion in NaTFSI (or NaFSI) has a corrosive effect on the aluminum foil collector. $^{[8]}$ Thus, it is of great significance to explore advanced salts to promote the wide applicability of SIBs. citations.quote: We have thoroughly examined its application as a single salt for the electrolytes of SIBs. The NaDFOB facilitates the formation of a dense and robust cathode-electrolyte interface (CEI) layer on the $\mathrm{Na_{3}Fe_{2}(PO_{4})P_{2}O_{7}}$ (NFPP) cathode, significantly enhances its cyclability and Coulombic efficiency (CE). Specifically, the NFPP electrode demonstrates an impressive capacity retention of 98.7% after 1000 cycles along with an average CE of 99.96%. To show the potential for low-temperature application, the NFPP electrodes with different electrolytes were tested at low temperatures. Notably, the NFPP electrode with NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte exhibits a capacity retention of 92.7% at -20 °C compared to that at 25 °C. Even at -40 °C, a high capacity retention of 84.8% is achieved (Figure 2g,h). Impressively, the NFPP electrode with the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte retains higher capacity retention than that with $NaPF_{6}-G2$ electrolyte at both -20 and -40 °C (Figures S6 and S7, Supporting Information). Moreover, the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte works well with other cathode materials. Both the $\mathrm{Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}}$ and $\mathrm{Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{2}F_{3}}$ electrodes show high cycling stability over 200 cycles (Figures S8 and S9, Supporting Information). Additionally, the compatibility of the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte with the hard carbon (HC) anode is also evaluated. The HC electrode has a large overpotential at room temperature and shows a small capacity (Figure S10, Supporting Information), which may be result of the thick SEI film on the Na metal surface slowing down the speed of sodium-ions passing through the SEI film and increase the polarization of the cell (Figure S11, Supporting Information). $^{[8]}$

To avoid the influence of the high polarization from Na metal, HC//NFPP full coin-cells were assembled.

The NaDFOB facilitates the formation of a dense and robust cathode-electrolyte interface (CEI) layer on the $\mathrm{Na_{3}Fe_{2}(PO_{4})P_{2}O_{7}}$ (NFPP) cathode, significantly enhances its cyclability and Coulombic efficiency (CE). Specifically, the NFPP electrode demonstrates an impressive capacity retention of 98.7% after 1000 cycles along with an average CE of 99.96%. Moreover, the hard carbon (HC)//NFPP pouch cell with NaDFOB-diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (G2) electrolyte shows an extended cycling lifespan of 500 cycles and commendable low-temperature performance. Our findings contribute to the exploration of affordable and functional sodium salts, thereby advancing the practical implementation of SIBs in various applications.

semantic_evidence_reviews.recommendation_reason: NaDFOB-G2 (1 M, additive-free) is directly supported as a viable low-temperature electrolyte and is compatible with NVP-family cathodes, so the electrolyte selection portion is partly supported. However, the core target quantity (reversible no-plating capacity limit for Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3||hard-carbon at -20 C) is unaddressed, no recorded_tool_predictions were produced, and hard-carbon compatibility is flagged as problematic; therefore a hold is warranted pending direct full-cell/no-plating evidence.

citations.quote: Kang's group $^{[48]}$ evaluated the electrochemical behavior of graphite electrodes using various glymes, i.e., TEGDME, DEGDME, and DME, as solvents and NaPF $_6$ , NaClO $_4$ , and NaCF $_3$ SO $_3$ salts. The results clearly highlighted that, while the salt has negligible influence, the solvent plays a key role on both intercalation potential and rate capability. An increase of the glyme molecular weight was found to increase the intercalation potential but decreasing the rate capability. The NaPF $_6$ in DEGDME electrolyte was selected for the realization of a full cell in combination with Na $_{1.5}$ VPO $_{4.8}$ F $_{0.7}$ cathode, characterized by a working voltage of 3 V, capacity of 45 mAh g $^{-1}$ (with respect to the mass of both the electrodes), good rate capability and promising capacity retention (80% after 250 cycles). $^{[48]}$ The correlation between the glyme molecular weight with the intercalation potential and the rate capability was later confirmed by Jache and co-workers. $^{[49]}$ Kang's group $^{[50]}$ investigated the solvated Na $^+$ intercalation mechanism using operando X-ray diffraction analysis, electrochemical titration, real-time optical observation, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations.

citations.chunk_id: 0002_Cai 等 - 2024 - A dual-functional electrolyte additive for stabilizing the solid electrolyte interphase and solvatio::sec3::child1
citations.quote:
As is well known, sodium salts, a medium for ion conductivity and sodium sources for sothiation/de-sothiation process, plays an essential role in determining the electrochemical performance of SIBs. Therefore,

Ming [3] et al. evaluated the properties of sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ), sodium perchlorate (NaClO $_4$ ), sodium trifluoromethanesulfonate (NaOTF) and sodium tetrafluoroborate (NaBF $_4$ ) as main salts. Among them, NaPF $_6$ was proven to have the best comprehensive performance including high solubility, high thermal stability and optimized orbital energy level. The compatibility of sodium salts and solvents/additives is considerably important for the function of the sodium salts. Generally, the solvents with additives are mainly used as a medium to transport sodium ions, affecting the conductivity and viscosity of the electrolyte, solvating the electrolyte salts, and ensuring the transmission of sodium ions. Yi et al. [4] incorporated a HC anode protected by ester-originated SEI with ether-based electrolyte, which indeed fused the merits of ester- and ether-based electrolytes and achieved a high reversibility and rate capability. Che et al. [5] systematically studied the carbonate-based electrolytes for NFM/HC SIBs and demonstrated that as compared with ethylene carbonate (EC)-based electrolyte, Propylene carbonate (PC)-based electrolytes outperform better in terms of capacity retention and safety.

requirements.requirement: Salt concentration 0.8 mol/L NaPF6
requirements.reasoning: The source's ECC formulation is explicitly given as 0.8 M NaPF6 in EC/PC/EMC, matching the candidate's 0.8 M NaPF6 concentration.

citations.chunk_id: 0002_Cai 等 - 2024 - A dual-functional electrolyte additive for stabilizing the solid electrolyte interphase and solvatio::sec7::child9
citations.quote: As a recent upstart in the field of energy storage, the energy storage efficiency of SIBs under high temperature conditions is one of the main research focuses. Capacity retention of the SIBs with/without NaDFP after 7 days, 14 days, and 28 days of shelving under 60 °C are shown in the Fig. 4c. Capacity retention of the batteries with NaDFP remains 83 % after 14 days. Even after 28 days, it still remains a capacity of 69 %. These results show that the cells with NaDFP exhibit less energy loss after each pause as compared to the baseline, apparently meaning less anodic decomposition of the electrolyte, less CEI dissolution/repair, and/or less ions dissolution. In addition to high temperature, battery stability at high voltages is also affected by EC oxidation. As shown in the Fig. 4d, the capacity retention of battery with NaDFP slightly improved under 60 °C, 4 V after 150 cycles. In previous work, it was found that PC has better cycling stability at the cathode electrodes. Therefore, in order to obtain better cycle performance, EC was partially replaced by PC while NaDFP being introduced as shown in Fig. 4e (ECC-0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ EC/PC/EMC = 0.5:2:0.5). Moreover, in order to understand the dissolution behavior of transition metals in the NFM cathodes with and without NaDFP, the amount of transition metals deposited on the hard carbon anodes after 100 cycles at 45 °C was measured by ICP-OES [19]. Lower contents of Ni and Fe were detected on the anode with NaDFP.

requirements.requirement: Solvent composition EC/PC/EMC with PC as the dominant component (ratios ~1:4:1)
requirements.reasoning: The source describes ECC electrolyte with EC/PC/EMC = 0.5:2:0.5 (i.e., 1:4:1), which is equivalent to the candidate's EC:PC:EMC = 0.1667:0.6667:0.1667; EC is partially replaced by PC to obtain better cycle performance, consistent with the candidate's PC-rich ratio.

evidence_ledger.quote: Coin cells (CR2032) were used to test the electrochemical performances. 1M NaClO $_{4}$ solution in a mixture of ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume) was applied as the electrolyte for the half cell and full cells. Two pieces of Whatman glass fibers soaked with the electrolyte were used as the separator between the positive and negative electrode. The HC electrode was prepared by casting a slurry of 90 wt% HC, 5 wt% conductive carbon black and 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder on copper foil. In companions, electrodes using carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) and sodium alginate (NaAg) as the binder were also prepared. Typical loading mass of the HC electrode was around 1.5 mg cm $^{-2}$ . For the full cell, Na $_{3.5}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{2}$ F $_{3}$ powders were mixed with 20% carbon SP for the preparation of positive electrodes. The weight ratio of the positive/negative electrodes was 2.5. The cells were galvanostatic charged/discharged with a LAND 2001 CT battery test system (Wuhan, China) under various voltage ranges and current rates. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a VMP system (Biologic S.A., Claix, France).

evidence_ledger.quote: In view of this, there are few studies for low temperature NIBs using hard carbon as the anode. Instead, more attention is attracted to the alloy or carbon/alloy composite for their adequate capacity of around 100 mAh g $^{-1}$ at low temperatures, such as Ti-based metal oxides, $^{[16,17]}$ , Se/graphene $^{[18]}$ and Sb/CNT $^{[19]}$ composites. However, these anode materials are accompanied by the high average voltage, which is detrimental to the energy density of the full cell. Previous work indicates that the capacity of hard carbon may be fully utilized by lowering the cut-off potential to below 0 V. $^{[20]}$ It indeed allows a high capacity of 265 mAh g $^{-1}$ at -15 °C, $^{[21]}$ although the possibility of Na plating requires prudent investigation. In this work, the calcination protocol of synthesizing HC from biomass waste is systematically explored. It shows a significant dependence of the performance on the heat treatment processes. The optimized HC was then evaluated at both the room and low-temperature. Assisted with the in situ and ex situ XRD, the possibility of Na metal plating is thoroughly examined. A safe and reversible capacity of 250 mAh g $^{-1}$ at -20 °C for HC is obtained without Na plating in HC. Furthermore, a $Na_{3.5}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{2}F_{3}$ cathode was prepared to couple with HC for investigating the low temperature behaviors of HC in full cell, which has been rarely studied.

evidence_ledger.quote: One may still argue the accuracy of in situ XRD tests as the signal of metallic Na would not be detectable until the amount is accumulated to a specific value. In order to determine the Na plating capacity more punctually, ex situ XRD is conducted on HC electrodes in coin cells with capacity limitation from 200 to $300\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ . The cells were cycled for 10 cycles to accumulate potential metallic Na. XRD patterns were collected at a discharged state. As shown in Figure S4, no Na peak is observed beneath the capacity of $250\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ , and the Na signal appeared in $300\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ sample. The Coulombic efficiency provides implications. The average Coulombic efficiency is around $97.4\%$ for the cells cycling at a limited capacity of $250\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ or less. The value is close to $97.8\%$ when the cell is tested at room temperature with a cut-off voltage of 0 V. evidence_ledger.quote: We argue that tuning the solvation structure through introducing solvents with various solvation capability could enhance the solubility of salt by decreasing the system degree of order ( $\Delta S > 0$ ) at low temperature. More specifically, mixing an SS solvent and a WS solvent could have more diverse solvation structure that is capable of altering spontaneously in response to the temperature dropping, and thus, realizing a temperature-adaptive electrolyte (Figure 1b). As a proof of concept, we selected $NaPF_{6}$ as a representative salt to pair with an SS–WS ether solvent mixture. To minimize any potential impact of $\varepsilon$ and DN on the solvation structure, DIG and tetrahydrofuran (THF) solvents with similar $\varepsilon$ (7.23 vs 7.58) and DN (19.5 vs 20.0 kcal mol $^{-1}$ ) values, $^{[15,16]}$ were specifically chosen as the SS and WS solvents, respectively (Table S1, Supporting Information). To compare, 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in THF (denoted as NT) was chosen as the WS electrolyte and 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in DIG (denoted as ND) as the SS electrolyte. We then used density functional theory (DFT) calculations to determine the binding energies $(E_{\mathrm{b}})$ of cation–solvent complexes based on the optimized geometrical structures (Figure S1, Supporting Information).

evidence_ledger.paper_id: 0070_Xia 等 - 2025 - Sodium-DifluorooxalatoBorate-Based Electrolytes for Long-Term Cycle Life and Enhanced Low-Temperat
evidence_ledger.quote:
Miaomiao Xia, Hui Chen, Zhenxu Zheng, Qingfei Meng, $^{*}$ Along Zhao, Xiaoyang Chen, Xinping Ai, Yongjin Fang, $^{*}$ and Yuliang Cao $^{*}$

Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) are emerging as a promising alternative for next-generation energy storage solutions, driven by the economic and environmental benefits of abundant sodium resources. A pivotal aspect of SIB advancement is the development of advanced electrolytes, which remains a formidable challenge. Herein, a facile and scalable synthesis method for low-cost sodium-difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB) is reported and explored its application as a standalone electrolyte salt for SIBs. The NaDFOB-based ether electrolyte demonstrates exceptional electrochemical stability, solvent compatibility, and the unique capacity to form a dense, robust solid-electrolyte interphase layer on electrode surfaces. As a result, the $\mathrm{Na_{4}Fe_{3}(PO_{4})_{2}P_{2}O_{7}}$ (NFPP) cathode with NaDFOB-based electrolyte exhibits ultrahigh cycling stability with a remarkable capacity retention of 98.7% after 1000 cycles. Furthermore, an Ah-level hard carbon (HC)//NFPP pouch cell using NaDFOB-based ether electrolyte shows an impressive cycle life of 500 cycles, coupled with an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.9%. The pouch cells also maintain superior electrochemical performance across a broad temperature range from -40 to 60 °C, showcasing the electrolyte's versatility.

evidence_ledger.quote:
Zheng Tang $^{+}$ , Hong Wang $^{+}$ , Peng-Fei Wu, Si-Yu Zhou, Yuan-Cheng Huang, Rui Zhang, Dan Sun, $^{*}$ You-Gen Tang, and Hai-Yan Wang $^{*}$

Abstract: Sodium-ion batteries capable of operating at rate and temperature extremes are highly desirable, but elusive due to the dynamics and thermodynamics limitations. Herein, a strategy of electrode-electrolyte interfacial chemistry modulation is proposed. The commercial hard carbon demonstrates superior rate performance with $212\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ at an ultra-high current density of $5\ A\ g^{-1}$ in the electrolyte with weak ion solvation/desolvation, which is much higher than those in common electrolytes (nearly no capacity in carbonate-based electrolytes). Even at $-20^{\circ}C$ , a high capacity of $175\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ (74% of its room-temperature capacity) can be maintained at $2\ A\ g^{-1}$ . Such an electrode retains 90% of its initial capacity after 1000 cycles. As proven, weak ion solvation/desolvation of tetrahydrofuran greatly facilitates fast-ion diffusion at the SEI/electrolyte interface and homogeneous SEI with well-distributed NaF and organic components ensures fast $Na^{+}$ diffusion through the SEI layer and a stable interface.

evidence_ledger.quote: In summary, we have demonstrated that electrode-electrolyte interphase chemistry including ion desolvation and SEI interphase are crucial to the electrochemical properties of the anode at the ultra-high rate and low-temperature extremes via the comparative study of different electrolytes. The THF-based electrolyte enables the commercial HC anode superior rate capability (up to $5 \, Ag^{-1}$ ) and ultra-low-temperature performance (operating stably at $-20^{\circ}C$ ). Kinetic analysis reveals that the remarkable performance is attributed to weakly $Na^{+}$ -solvent desolvation energy and uniform SEI composition achieved in the THF-based electrolyte, which is beneficial to the ion diffusion between the electrolyte–electrode interface and interface stability. This work not only proposes an advanced low-temperature electrolyte, but also provides new insights into the interfacial modulation for next-generation high-rate and low-temperature batteries.

As is well known, sodium salts, a medium for ion conductivity and sodium sources for sothiation/de-sothiation process, plays an essential role in determining the electrochemical performance of SIBs. Therefore,

Ming [3] et al. evaluated the properties of sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ), sodium perchlorate (NaClO $_4$ ), sodium trifluoromethanesulfonate (NaOTF) and sodium tetrafluoroborate (NaBF $_4$ ) as main salts. Among them, NaPF $_6$ was proven to have the best comprehensive performance including high solubility, high thermal stability and optimized orbital energy level. The compatibility of sodium salts and solvents/additives is considerably important for the function of the sodium salts. Generally, the solvents with additives are mainly used as a medium to transport sodium ions, affecting the conductivity and viscosity of the electrolyte, solvating the electrolyte salts, and ensuring the transmission of sodium ions. Yi et al. [4] incorporated a HC anode protected by ester-originated SEI with ether-based electrolyte, which indeed fused the merits of ester- and ether-based electrolytes and achieved a high reversibility and rate capability. Che et al. [5] systematically studied the carbonate-based electrolytes for NFM/HC SIBs and demonstrated that as compared with ethylene carbonate (EC)-based electrolyte, Propylene carbonate (PC)-based electrolytes outperform better in terms of capacity retention and safety.

citations.quote: Coin cells (CR2032) were used to test the electrochemical performances. 1M NaClO $_{4}$ solution in a mixture of ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume) was applied as the electrolyte for the half cell and full cells. Two pieces of Whatman glass fibers soaked with the electrolyte were used as the separator between the positive and negative electrode. The HC electrode was prepared by casting a slurry of 90 wt% HC, 5 wt% conductive carbon black and 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder on copper foil. In companions, electrodes using carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) and sodium alginate (NaAg) as the binder were also prepared. Typical loading mass of the HC electrode was around 1.5 mg cm $^{-2}$ . For the full cell, Na $_{3.5}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{2}$ F $_{3}$ powders were mixed with 20% carbon SP for the preparation of positive electrodes. The weight ratio of the positive/negative electrodes was 2.5. The cells were galvanostatic charged/discharged with a LAND 2001 CT battery test system (Wuhan, China) under various voltage ranges and current rates. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a VMP system (Biologic S.A., Claix, France).

Coin cells (CR2032) were used to test the electrochemical performances. 1M NaClO $_{4}$ solution in a mixture of ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume) was applied as the electrolyte for the half cell and full cells. Two pieces of Whatman glass fibers soaked with the electrolyte were used as the separator between the positive and negative electrode. The HC electrode was prepared by casting a slurry of 90 wt% HC, 5 wt% conductive carbon black and 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder on copper foil. In companions, electrodes using carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) and sodium alginate (NaAg) as the binder were also prepared. Typical loading mass of the HC electrode was around 1.5 mg cm $^{-2}$ . For the full cell, Na $_{3.5}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{2}$ F $_{3}$ powders were mixed with 20% carbon SP for the preparation of positive electrodes. The weight ratio of the positive/negative electrodes was 2.5. The cells were galvanostatic charged/discharged with a LAND 2001 CT battery test system (Wuhan, China) under various voltage ranges and current rates. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a VMP system (Biologic S.A., Claix, France).

Zheng Tang $^{+}$ , Hong Wang $^{+}$ , Peng-Fei Wu, Si-Yu Zhou, Yuan-Cheng Huang, Rui Zhang, Dan Sun, $^{*}$ You-Gen Tang, and Hai-Yan Wang $^{*}$

Abstract: Sodium-ion batteries capable of operating at rate and temperature extremes are highly desirable, but elusive due to the dynamics and thermodynamics limitations. Herein, a strategy of electrode-electrolyte interfacial chemistry modulation is proposed. The commercial hard carbon demonstrates superior rate performance with $212\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ at an ultra-high current density of $5\ A\ g^{-1}$ in the electrolyte with weak ion solvation/desolvation, which is much higher than those in common electrolytes (nearly no capacity in carbonate-based electrolytes). Even at $-20^{\circ}C$ , a high capacity of $175\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ (74% of its room-temperature capacity) can be maintained at $2\ A\ g^{-1}$ . Such an electrode retains 90% of its initial capacity after 1000 cycles. As proven, weak ion solvation/desolvation of tetrahydrofuran greatly facilitates fast-ion diffusion at the SEI/electrolyte interface and homogeneous SEI with well-distributed NaF and organic components ensures fast $Na^{+}$ diffusion through the SEI layer and a stable interface.

citations.quote: In summary, we have demonstrated that electrode-electrolyte interphase chemistry including ion desolvation and SEI interphase are crucial to the electrochemical properties of the anode at the ultra-high rate and low-temperature extremes via the comparative study of different electrolytes. The THF-based electrolyte enables the commercial HC anode superior rate capability (up to $5 \, Ag^{-1}$ ) and ultra-low-temperature performance (operating stably at $-20^{\circ}C$ ). Kinetic analysis reveals that the remarkable performance is attributed to weakly $Na^{+}$ -solvent desolvation energy and uniform SEI composition achieved in the THF-based electrolyte, which is beneficial to the ion diffusion between the electrolyte–electrode interface and interface stability. This work not only proposes an advanced low-temperature electrolyte, but also provides new insights into the interfacial modulation for next-generation high-rate and low-temperature batteries.

However, the full cells employing 1.0-P-E/M or 1.0-P-D exhibit rapid deterioration as temperature decreases. In contrast, the cell with 0.5-P-D maintains a high specific capacity of 85 mAh g $^{-1}$ at -20 °C (85% of the room temperature capacity) and 56 mAh g $^{-1}$ even under -40 °C (Figure S16, Supporting Information). Furthermore, the cycling stability of the three electrolytes at -20 °C was investigated (Figure 2e). The capacity of NLNMO||HC full cells with 1.0-P-E/M and 1.0-P-D exhibits a rapid decay until failure, whereas 0.5-P-D demonstrates a capacity retention of up to 89.65% after 50 cycles at 0.1 C. To investigate the interfacial kinetics, the Tafel curves of the HC||HC symmetric cells in different electrolytes were employed to assess the exchange current density ( $J_0$ ). The results suggest the $J_0$ of 0.5-P-D (0.017 mA cm $^{-2}$ ) is much higher than those of 1.0-P-D (0.009 mA cm $^{-2}$ ) and 1.0-P-E-M (0.004 mA cm $^{-2}$ ), indicating the facilitated kinetics in 0.5-P-D (Figure 2f). Moreover, temperature-dependent electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was conducted to further investigate the interfacial kinetics (Figure S17 and Tables S4–S6, Supporting Information).

association_citations.quote: Figure 1a and Table S1 (Supporting Information) present the temperature-dependent ionic conductivities of the dilute NaPF $_{6}$ -based ether electrolyte (0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ in DEGDME, 0.5-P-D), the conventional concentration NaPF $_{6}$ -based ether electrolyte (1.0 M NaPF $_{6}$ in DEGDME, 1.0-P-D), and the commercial ester-based electrolyte (1.0 M NaPF $_{6}$ in the mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC) and dimethyl carbonate (DMC) with a volume ratio of 1:1, 1.0-P-E/M). At 25 °C, 0.5-P-D exhibits a lower ionic conductivity (2.7 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) compared to 1.0-P-D (7.3 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) and 1.0-P-E/M (15.3 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) due to its low salt concentration. Over the temperature range from 25 to -50 °C, all three electrolytes display a negative correlation between ionic conductivity and temperature. However, the higher freezing points (Figure S1, Supporting Information) and steep increase in viscosity at low temperatures (Figures S2 and S3, Supporting Information) lead to decreased fluidity and even solidification of the 1.0-P-D and 1.0-P-E/M electrolytes, resulting in a sharp decline in ionic conductivity below 0 °C. In contrast, 0.5-P-D still exhibits a high value of 0.45 mS cm $^{-1}$ even at -50 °C, enabling considerable Na $^{+}$ migration in the liquid electrolyte at low temperatures. The coordination environments in the 0.5-P-D, 1.0-P-D, and 1.0-P-E/M electrolytes were characterized by Raman spectroscopy (Figure 1b).

citations.quote: The electrochemical performance was tested by CR2032 coin-type. The working electrodes were prepared by mixing 70 wt% active material, 20 wt% acetylene black and 10 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF). The slurry was coated on carbon-coated the Al foil and dried at 60 °C for 12 h in vacuum oven to obtain the testing electrodes. Two electrolytes were used for electrochemical tests. The dual-anion regulated electrolyte was prepared consisting of 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ and 0.2 M NaBF $_{4}$ in diethyleneglycol dimethyl ether. The electrolyte of 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ in propylene carbonate (PC) was selected as the reference electrolyte. The loading mass of the active material in the electrode was about 1.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ . The anode was pure Na metal foil and the separator was glass fiber (GF/D). The full cell was assembled by using HM-NVPF@CN cathode and hard carbon (HC) anode in BPG electrolyte. Before assembling the full cell, the hard carbon anode was pre-cycled for several cycles to form a stable electrode-electrolyte interface. Galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD) and galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) tests were conducted on a Neware system (CT-4008T-5V10mA-164, Shenzhen, China).

citations.chunk_id: 0073_Yang 等 - 2023 - Entropy-Driven Solvation toward Low-Temperature Sodium-Ion Batteries with Temperature-Adaptive Featu::sec2::child1
citations.quote: We argue that tuning the solvation structure through introducing solvents with various solvation capability could enhance the solubility of salt by decreasing the system degree of order ( $\Delta S > 0$ ) at low temperature. More specifically, mixing an SS solvent and a WS solvent could have more diverse solvation structure that is capable of altering spontaneously in response to the temperature dropping, and thus, realizing a temperature-adaptive electrolyte (Figure 1b). As a proof of concept, we selected $NaPF_{6}$ as a representative salt to pair with an SS–WS ether solvent mixture. To minimize any potential impact of $\varepsilon$ and DN on the solvation structure, DIG and tetrahydrofuran (THF) solvents with similar $\varepsilon$ (7.23 vs 7.58) and DN (19.5 vs 20.0 kcal mol $^{-1}$ ) values, $^{[15,16]}$ were specifically chosen as the SS and WS solvents, respectively (Table S1, Supporting Information). We first optimized our proposed SS–WS electrolyte formulation to 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in DIG and THF (2:8 in volume ratio, denoted as NDT, Figure S5, Supporting Information). To compare, 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in THF (denoted as NT) was chosen as the WS electrolyte and 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in DIG (denoted as ND) as the SS electrolyte. We then used density functional theory (DFT) calculations to determine the binding energies $(E_{\mathrm{b}})$ of cation–solvent complexes based on the optimized geometrical structures (Figure S1, Supporting Information).

citations.quote:
2.4. Toward Practical Viability
We have also examined the compatibility of NDT electrolyte against high-voltage cathode materials for Na-ion batteries. A P2-type $Na_{2/3}Ni_{1/4}Cu_{1/12}Mn_{2/3}O_{2}$ (NNCM) cathode (Figure S16, Supporting Information) was selected as cathode materials to pair with Na metal anode in NDT electrolyte to assembled coin cells. With temperature dropping to -40 and -50 °C, NNCM cathode still achieves quite decent capacities of 79.7 and 72.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ , respectively, corresponding to 88.8% and 81.0% of the capacity delivered at 25 °C (Figure S17a, Supporting Information). Equally importantly, NNCM cathode demonstrated encouraging cycling stability and rate performance in NDT electrolytes under low-temperature operation. For instance, a high-capacity retention of 99.9% over 100 cycles with average columbic efficiency of 99.8% is achieved at -40 °C (Figure S17b, Supporting Information). Even at high rate of 2C, the NNCM cathode still retains reversible capacities of 74.5 mAh g $^{-1}$ (84.2% of that at 0.1 C, see Figure S17c, Supporting Information) at -40 °C. To further verify the feasibility of NDT electrolyte in practical cells, full cells with NNCM cathode and hard carbon anode were fabricated and cycled within 1.50–3.65 V at various temperatures. The NNCM||hard carbon cell delivers an initial discharge capacity of 71.2 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 25 °C, while 70.2% of that capacity can be maintained when the temperature decreases to -40 °C (Figure S18, Supporting Information). In addition, the NNCM||hard carbon full cell exhibits much enhanced cycling stability at -40 °C by featuring a 90.6% capacity retention after 400 cycles (Figure S17d, Supporting Information). Clearly, our testing data demonstrated NDT electrolyte is fully compatible with layered oxide cathode and hard carbon anode, and thus, showed great potential for practical applications in Na-ion battery.

To expand the generality of the concept, we constructed a series of SS–WS electrolyte by selecting linear ethers including 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) and triethylene glycol monomethyl ether (Triglyme) as SS solvents and cyclic ethers such as THF and 2-methyltetrahydrofuran (mTHF) as WS solvents. Four electrolyte solutions, namely, 1.0 M NaPF $_{6}$ DME/THF (NMT), 1.0 M NaPF $_{6}$ DME/mTHF (NMM), 1.0 M NaPF $_{6}$ Triglyme/mTHF (NTrT), and 1.0 M NaPF $_{6}$ DIG/mTHF (NDM)

We have also examined the compatibility of NDT electrolyte against high-voltage cathode materials for Na-ion batteries. A P2-type $Na_{2/3}Ni_{1/4}Cu_{1/12}Mn_{2/3}O_{2}$ (NNCM) cathode (Figure S16, Supporting Information) was selected as cathode materials to pair with Na metal anode in NDT electrolyte to assembled coin cells. With temperature dropping to -40 and -50 °C, NNCM cathode still achieves quite decent capacities of 79.7 and 72.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ , respectively, corresponding to 88.8% and 81.0% of the capacity delivered at 25 °C (Figure S17a, Supporting Information). Equally importantly, NNCM cathode demonstrated encouraging cycling stability and rate performance in NDT electrolytes under low-temperature operation. For instance, a high-capacity retention of 99.9% over 100 cycles with average columbic efficiency of 99.8% is achieved at -40 °C (Figure S17b, Supporting Information). To show the potential for low-temperature application, the NFPP electrodes with different electrolytes were tested at low temperatures. Notably, the NFPP electrode with NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte exhibits a capacity retention of 92.7% at -20 °C compared to that at 25 °C. Even at -40 °C, a high capacity retention of 84.8% is achieved (Figure 2g,h). Impressively, the NFPP electrode with the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte retains higher capacity retention than that with $NaPF_{6}-G2$ electrolyte at both -20 and -40 °C (Figures S6 and S7, Supporting Information). Moreover, the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte works well with other cathode materials. Both the $\mathrm{Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}}$ and $\mathrm{Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{2}F_{3}}$ electrodes show high cycling stability over 200 cycles (Figures S8 and S9, Supporting Information). Additionally, the compatibility of the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte with the hard carbon (HC) anode is also evaluated. The HC electrode has a large overpotential at room temperature and shows a small capacity (Figure S10, Supporting Information), which may be result of the thick SEI film on the Na metal surface slowing down the speed of sodium-ions passing through the SEI film and increase the polarization of the cell (Figure S11, Supporting Information). $^{[8]}$

To avoid the influence of the high polarization from Na metal, HC//NFPP full coin-cells were assembled.

citations.quote: Kang's group $^{[48]}$ evaluated the electrochemical behavior of graphite electrodes using various glymes, i.e., TEGDME, DEGDME, and DME, as solvents and NaPF $_6$ , NaClO $_4$ , and NaCF $_3$ SO $_3$ salts. The results clearly highlighted that, while the salt has negligible influence, the solvent plays a key role on both intercalation potential and rate capability. An increase of the glyme molecular weight was found to increase the intercalation potential but decreasing the rate capability. The NaPF $_6$ in DEGDME electrolyte was selected for the realization of a full cell in combination with Na $_{1.5}$ VPO $_{4.8}$ F $_{0.7}$ cathode, characterized by a working voltage of 3 V, capacity of 45 mAh g $^{-1}$ (with respect to the mass of both the electrodes), good rate capability and promising capacity retention (80% after 250 cycles). $^{[48]}$ The correlation between the glyme molecular weight with the intercalation potential and the rate capability was later confirmed by Jache and co-workers. $^{[49]}$ Kang's group $^{[50]}$ investigated the solvated Na $^+$ intercalation mechanism using operando X-ray diffraction analysis, electrochemical titration, real-time optical observation, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations.

citations.quote:
As is well known, sodium salts, a medium for ion conductivity and sodium sources for sothiation/de-sothiation process, plays an essential role in determining the electrochemical performance of SIBs. Therefore,

Ming [3] et al. evaluated the properties of sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ), sodium perchlorate (NaClO $_4$ ), sodium trifluoromethanesulfonate (NaOTF) and sodium tetrafluoroborate (NaBF $_4$ ) as main salts. Among them, NaPF $_6$ was proven to have the best comprehensive performance including high solubility, high thermal stability and optimized orbital energy level. The compatibility of sodium salts and solvents/additives is considerably important for the function of the sodium salts. Generally, the solvents with additives are mainly used as a medium to transport sodium ions, affecting the conductivity and viscosity of the electrolyte, solvating the electrolyte salts, and ensuring the transmission of sodium ions. Yi et al. [4] incorporated a HC anode protected by ester-originated SEI with ether-based electrolyte, which indeed fused the merits of ester- and ether-based electrolytes and achieved a high reversibility and rate capability. Che et al. [5] systematically studied the carbonate-based electrolytes for NFM/HC SIBs and demonstrated that as compared with ethylene carbonate (EC)-based electrolyte, Propylene carbonate (PC)-based electrolytes outperform better in terms of capacity retention and safety.

requirements.reasoning: The source's ECC formulation is explicitly given as 0.8 M NaPF6 in EC/PC/EMC, matching the candidate's 0.8 M NaPF6 concentration.

citations.quote: As a recent upstart in the field of energy storage, the energy storage efficiency of SIBs under high temperature conditions is one of the main research focuses. Capacity retention of the SIBs with/without NaDFP after 7 days, 14 days, and 28 days of shelving under 60 °C are shown in the Fig. 4c. Capacity retention of the batteries with NaDFP remains 83 % after 14 days. Even after 28 days, it still remains a capacity of 69 %. These results show that the cells with NaDFP exhibit less energy loss after each pause as compared to the baseline, apparently meaning less anodic decomposition of the electrolyte, less CEI dissolution/repair, and/or less ions dissolution. In addition to high temperature, battery stability at high voltages is also affected by EC oxidation. As shown in the Fig. 4d, the capacity retention of battery with NaDFP slightly improved under 60 °C, 4 V after 150 cycles. In previous work, it was found that PC has better cycling stability at the cathode electrodes. Therefore, in order to obtain better cycle performance, EC was partially replaced by PC while NaDFP being introduced as shown in Fig. 4e (ECC-0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ EC/PC/EMC = 0.5:2:0.5). Moreover, in order to understand the dissolution behavior of transition metals in the NFM cathodes with and without NaDFP, the amount of transition metals deposited on the hard carbon anodes after 100 cycles at 45 °C was measured by ICP-OES [19]. Lower contents of Ni and Fe were detected on the anode with NaDFP.

citations.chunk_id: 0036_Lin 等 - 2019 - Exploring room- and low-temperature performance of hard carbon material in half and full Na-ion batt::sec5::child0
citations.quote: Coin cells (CR2032) were used to test the electrochemical performances. 1M NaClO $_{4}$ solution in a mixture of ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume) was applied as the electrolyte for the half cell and full cells. Two pieces of Whatman glass fibers soaked with the electrolyte were used as the separator between the positive and negative electrode. The HC electrode was prepared by casting a slurry of 90 wt% HC, 5 wt% conductive carbon black and 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder on copper foil. In companions, electrodes using carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) and sodium alginate (NaAg) as the binder were also prepared. Typical loading mass of the HC electrode was around 1.5 mg cm $^{-2}$ . For the full cell, Na $_{3.5}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{2}$ F $_{3}$ powders were mixed with 20% carbon SP for the preparation of positive electrodes. The weight ratio of the positive/negative electrodes was 2.5. The cells were galvanostatic charged/discharged with a LAND 2001 CT battery test system (Wuhan, China) under various voltage ranges and current rates. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a VMP system (Biologic S.A., Claix, France).

citations.chunk_id: 0062_Tang 等 - 2022 - ElectrodeElectrolyte Interfacial Chemistry Modulation for Ultra-High Rate Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec2::child4
citations.quote: This work aims to demonstrate the critical effect of electrode-electrolyte interfacial chemistry on the performance of a commercial hard carbon anode operating at the rate and temperature extremes. A new weakly solvating electrolyte (WSE) consisting of a cyclic ether (tetrahydrofuran, THF) as solvent and $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ as the electrolyte salt was proposed to optimize the interfacial properties of anode/electrolyte. Surprisingly, the lower ion desolvation energy and homogeneous SEI are simultaneously achieved. Benefiting from the low $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ desolvation energy and fast transport at the anode/electrolyte interface, the commercial hard carbon anode demonstrates ultra-high rate capability and remarkable low-temperature performance.

citations.quote: It is well known that low-temperature performance is also significant for some special scenarios in practical applications. However, there are few reports on the low-temperature performance of the HC anode for SIBs. As previous studies have indicated that the solvation structure of the electrolyte defines the charge-transfer behavior at low temperature, $^{[13a]}$ the low-temperature performance of HC in THF-based electrolyte was further investigated. When the ambient temperature drops to $-5^{\circ}C$ (Figure 5a), the specific capacities of HC in 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ /THF electrolyte at 20 mA g $^{-1}$ and 5 Ag $^{-1}$ are 282 and 155 mAh g $^{-1}$ , respectively, indicating superior rate capability. Even at -20°C, a high capacity of 269 and 175 mAh g $^{-1}$ can be achieved at 20 mA g $^{-1}$ and 2 Ag $^{-1}$ , respectively. The charge-discharge profile in 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ /THF electrolyte (Figure 5b,c) still maintains a high low-plateau capacity at different densities, indicating favorable kinetics. Moreover, HC anode in 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ /THF electrolyte also possesses superior long-term cycling stability with a specific capacity of 203 mAh g $^{-1}$ over 1000 cycles at a large current density of 2 A g $^{-1}$ at -5°C (Figure 5d). Even at a lower temperature of -20°C, it still delivers high capacity retention up to 95% with a specific capacity of 181 mAh g $^{-1}$ over 1000 cycles (Figure 5e).

citations.quote:
Zheng Tang $^{+}$ , Hong Wang $^{+}$ , Peng-Fei Wu, Si-Yu Zhou, Yuan-Cheng Huang, Rui Zhang, Dan Sun, $^{*}$ You-Gen Tang, and Hai-Yan Wang $^{*}$

Abstract: Sodium-ion batteries capable of operating at rate and temperature extremes are highly desirable, but elusive due to the dynamics and thermodynamics limitations. Herein, a strategy of electrode-electrolyte interfacial chemistry modulation is proposed. The commercial hard carbon demonstrates superior rate performance with $212\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ at an ultra-high current density of $5\ A\ g^{-1}$ in the electrolyte with weak ion solvation/desolvation, which is much higher than those in common electrolytes (nearly no capacity in carbonate-based electrolytes). Even at $-20^{\circ}C$ , a high capacity of $175\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ (74% of its room-temperature capacity) can be maintained at $2\ A\ g^{-1}$ . Such an electrode retains 90% of its initial capacity after 1000 cycles. As proven, weak ion solvation/desolvation of tetrahydrofuran greatly facilitates fast-ion diffusion at the SEI/electrolyte interface and homogeneous SEI with well-distributed NaF and organic components ensures fast $Na^{+}$ diffusion through the SEI layer and a stable interface.
